chunks: Ahmad ibn Muhammad from Ibn Mahbub from Abu Ayyub from Muhammad ibn Muslim from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) said:
Whoever draws his weapon in a garrison city (misr) and kills, he is executed (qisas) and exiled from that city.
And whoever draws his weapon in non-garrison cities, strikes, kills, takes wealth, but does not kill, he is a muharib (warrior), and his penalty is the penalty of the muharib.
And his affair is referred to the Imam; if he wishes, he kills him; if he wishes, he crucifies him; if he wishes, he cuts his hand and foot.
He said: And if he strikes, kills, and takes wealth, it is upon the Imam to cut his right hand for theft, then hand him over to the heirs of the slain, who pursue him with the wealth, then kill him.
Abu Ubaydah said to him: May God improve you, tell me, if the heirs of the slain forgive him?
Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) said: If they forgive him, it is still upon the Imam to kill him, because he has fought God and His Messenger, killed, and stolen.
Then Abu Ubaydah said to him: Tell me, if the heirs of the slain wish to take the blood money (diyah) from him and let him go, is that for them?
He said: No, killing is upon him (i.e., he must be killed).
ai.seo_question: What is the difference in punishment for drawing weapons in a garrison city versus other cities according to Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Isfahani’s al-Ishtibār elaborates on the jurisprudence of *al-Muharib* (highway robber), distinguishing between *Qatl* (killing) and *Sariqah* (theft) to determine whether the punishment is discretionary (*Takhayyur*) for the Imam or mandatory (*Haqq Allah*). It highlights the Shia scholarly view that the crime against God (*Haqq Allah*) in killing and stealing persists even if the heirs (*Awliya*) forgive the perpetrator or accept blood money, ensuring the state enforces divine justice. The text underscores the Imam’s authority to impose crucifixion, exile, or execution based on the specific combination of acts committed.
